chapters.title: SHAP Values: Understand One Prediction
chapters.description: Start with a baseline, a prediction, and the feature contributions that connect them. A clear reading path through all nine A Data Odyssey videos.

chapters.title: Shapley Values: Work Out Each Person’s Share
chapters.description: Calculate contributions in every joining order, then derive the Shapley weights from a complete three-person example.

chapters.title: From Shapley Values to Model Explanations
chapters.description: Compute every partially known prediction in the playlist’s age-and-degree example, then connect the calculation to Kernel SHAP and Tree SHAP.

chapters.title: Calculate and Check SHAP Values in Python
chapters.description: Fit an Abalone regression model, choose a reference dataset, inspect the Explanation object, and verify the values before plotting them.

chapters.title: Read SHAP Plots One Question at a Time
chapters.description: Understand force, bar, beeswarm, and dependence plots using the same Abalone model and the same set of explained rows.

chapters.title: What a SHAP Explanation Can—and Cannot—Tell You
chapters.description: Understand implementation limits, dependent inputs, causal claims, and the temptation to turn model patterns into unsupported stories.

chapters.title: SHAP Violin Plots and Heatmaps
chapters.description: Use violin plots to read attribution distributions and heatmaps to compare groups of predictions, without confusing their color scales.

chapters.title: SHAP for Classification: Keep Track of the Output
chapters.description: Explain binary margins, probability outputs, and multiclass logits, with checks that reconstruct each model’s predictions.

chapters.title: Explain Categorical Features Without Losing Their Meaning
chapters.description: Understand one-hot contributions, when to sum them, and how CatBoost keeps a single attribution per original categorical input.

chapters.title: Explain Isolation Forest Anomalies with SHAP
chapters.description: Explain household electricity anomalies on the decision-score and path-length scales, with explicit sign conventions and reproducible calculations.
